title: Locked Boxes

post.author: u/wendmoor_clerk_mirembe
post.title: I'm the night clerk at a city lost-property office. Every backup from last year is there, every checksum matches, and not one will open.

blocks.text: I'm Mirembe, night clerk at the Wendmoor lost-property office. Each found item gets a record on our computer: what it is, where it was found, a photo, and the owner's name if known.
Our records are scrambled on the disk. Scrambling data with a key, so only the key's holder can read it, is encryption. Keeping data scrambled on a disk is encryption at rest.
TLS, short for Transport Layer Security, the padlock in your browser, scrambles data travelling over the internet: encryption in transit.

At 01:00 each night a backup job copies everything into a separate store: a spare copy to restore, or copy back, after a mistake. The store keeps the last 365 nights. Beside each backup sits a checksum, a short fingerprint of the file that stops matching if anything in it changes.
The job scrambles each backup with one key that both locks and unlocks, like my front-door key: a symmetric key. It kept it in a folder named keys, in the same store as the backups.
The other kind comes in pairs, like a post box: anyone can post a letter, but only the postman's key opens it. A public key locks; only its matching private key unlocks. That's an asymmetric pair.

Last October an audit asked us to rotate the backup key monthly, swapping in a fresh one so a leaked key stops locking new backups. Radoslav, the city's IT contractor, wrote a script, a small program. From 1 November 2025, at 00:30 on the 1st, it made a new key version, v2, then v3, for later backups. Then it deleted the version before.

Tonight at 22:40 Ms Desrosiers came to the window. Her grandfather's brass compass was handed in on 9 November last year. Unclaimed after 180 days, it went to the charity auction on 8 May, and its record and photo left our computer. She needs the photo to prove it's hers. Only the backups hold it.

I rang Radoslav on the city's night number. He tried to restore the 180 backups holding her photo, 10 November to 8 May, then newer ones. Each log line shows the backup's night, its checksum, the key version that locked it, and the result.

10 Nov 2025  checksum ok  key v2   not found
08 May 2026  checksum ok  key v8   not found
30 Sep 2026  checksum ok  key v12  not found
01 Oct 2026  checksum ok  key v13  opened

blocks.label: backup_store_14_oct.png

diagram.aria: Radoslav's sketch of the backup store on 14 October 2026. Top row: 17 backups from 15 to 31 October 2025, locked with key v1, which was deleted on 1 November 2025; 334 backups from November 2025 to September 2026, locked with v2 to v12, each deleted a month later; 14 backups from 1 to 14 October 2026, locked with v13, which open. Bottom row: the rotation script, which runs at 00:30 on the 1st, adds a version and deletes the old one, in the keys folder, which sits in the same store and holds only v13. A note says her photo is in 180 backups, locked with v2 to v8.

notes.text: her photo: 180 backups, v2 to v8

blocks.caption: Redrawn from Radoslav's sketch of the store on 14 October 2026. All 365 backups are there and every checksum matches. 17 were locked with v1, deleted on 1 November 2025, and 334 with v2 to v12, each deleted when the next arrived. Only the 14 made this month, under v13, open. Her photo is in 180 backups, under v2 to v8.

blocks.text: A checksum proves a file hasn't changed, not that anyone can open it. The folder holds only v13, from 1 October: 14 backups open, and 351 never will. The script's log said "old version removed" each month. Nothing alerted anyone, and nobody had restored a backup since its first run.
Every box is on the shelf, every seal unbroken, and no key fits.
Radoslav found a quieter problem. With the key beside the backups, anyone copying that one store got the boxes and the key together.

The city runs a key service: a separate, guarded service holding each department's main key, its master key. That key never leaves it. The service unlocks only for programs allowed to ask, and records each use.
Mr Valcourt, our manager, wants a fix before the script's next run on 1 November. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: A locked box with its key taped to the lid. Before you choose, answer three things. Where does each key version live? What happens to a version once a newer one exists? And when did anyone last take a backup all the way back to a photo on a screen? Doing that on a schedule is called a restore test. A backup nobody has opened is a hope, not a backup.

replies.author: u/wendmoor_clerk_mirembe
replies.text: Radoslav says the last full restore was a drill in September 2025, before the script existed. It worked. Since then, nobody tried.

comments.author: u/one_key_grishin
comments.text: Rotation is the risk. A key that never changes can never go missing. Turn the monthly script off, keep v13 for good, and every backup from tonight on opens. Audits love rotation; restores don't.

comments.author: u/city_it_radoslav
comments.text: Radoslav here. I'm sorry. I wrote the deleting step so old keys wouldn't lie about. The key service's guide offers envelope encryption. Each backup gets its own fresh key, a data key. The service locks that data key with the master key, and the locked data key is stored beside its backup, like a key in a sealed envelope only the service can open.

reply.prompt: Mr Valcourt wants a fix before the script's next run on 1 November. What should the office change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Stop rotating the backup key, so every backup from now on opens with the same key.
options.part2: Radoslav switched the monthly script off on Thursday, and key v13 stays for good. In the sim I set rotation to none and replayed from 31 October 2025: on 14 October 2026 all 365 backups open, and her photo opens in 180 of 180. But the key still sits in the same store, so one stolen copy of the store exposes 365 of 365, and one leaked key opens all 365 too, with nothing to retire it. In the real store the 351 lost backups stay lost. The next audit will ask why rotation stopped.
options.senior: Grishin fixed the loss by removing the protection. Rotation was never the mistake; deleting old versions was. A key that never changes lets one leak open every backup ever made with it, and this key still sits beside the backups, so one copied store is the whole archive. NIST SP 800-57 calls the time a key may be used its cryptoperiod, and splits it: a key stops locking new data after its originator-usage period but must still open old data for its recipient-usage period. Keep rotating; keep the old versions for opening; move the keys away from the data.

options.text: Test a restore of last month's backup every week, so a backup we cannot open is caught.
options.verdict: An early alarm, the same broken keys
options.part2: Radoslav set a test for every Sunday: restore the backup from 28 nights before and open one photo, and email him if it fails. In the sim I turned the tests on and replayed from 31 October 2025: the first test, on Sunday 2 November 2025, cannot open the backup of 5 October, locked with v1, deleted the day before. By tonight 46 of 52 tests fail. The alarm would have rung a year early, but a test changes nothing it finds: on 14 October 2026, 351 backups still cannot open, and the key still sits beside the backups, so one stolen copy of the store exposes 14 of 365.
options.senior: Restore tests are real practice and belong in every backup plan: a backup only counts once you have restored from it. Here a weekly test would have caught the deletion the day after the first run. But it detects; it doesn't design. The script would still delete every version, and the key would still sit beside the data. Pair the test with the fix: a key service that keeps old versions for opening, and keys held apart from what they protect.

options.text: Lock backups with a public key, and keep the private key on paper in the office safe.
options.verdict: Apart, but by hand and forever
options.part2: Radoslav made one key pair. The backup job keeps only the public key, which can lock but not open, and the private key is printed and locked in the office safe. In the sim I chose the office safe, no rotation, and replayed: 0 of 365 lost, and one stolen copy of the store exposes 0 of 365. But that one sheet opens all 365, it is never changed, and nothing records who opened the safe and typed it in. A restore means carrying the paper to a keyboard at night. If the sheet is lost or burns, every backup goes with it.
options.senior: Separating the key from the data is the right instinct, and an asymmetric pair is a real way to let a job lock what it can't open. But a paper key is managed by hand: it is never rotated, every use is invisible, it has to be typed into a computer to be used at all, and it is one copy away from losing everything. A key service gives the same separation with rotation, a record of each use, and old versions kept for opening.

options.text: Keep keys in a key service apart from the data, and keep old key versions for opening.
options.part2: Radoslav moved the backups onto the city's key service before the 1 November run, with envelope encryption: each backup gets its own data key, locked by the master key, and no version is ever deleted. The keys folder in the store is empty now. In the sim I chose a key service, monthly rotation keeping old versions, and envelope encryption, and replayed from 31 October 2025: on 14 October 2026 all 365 backups open, versions v1 to v13 are held, one stolen copy of the store exposes 0 of 365, one leaked data key opens 1 backup, and every use is on record. Her photo opens in 180 of 180. The real store can't be replayed: 351 backups stay shut, her photo among them. I wrote to Ms Desrosiers on Thursday. Radoslav added a weekly restore test as well.
options.senior: Rotate keys, never delete the versions old data needs, and keep keys somewhere the data isn't. A key service does all three: it holds master keys that never leave it, adds a new version on rotation while keeping the old ones for opening (AWS KMS keeps all key material until the key itself is deleted), and records every use. Envelope encryption makes it practical: each backup has its own data key, locked by the master key and stored beside the backup, so a stolen store holds only locked keys and one leaked data key opens one backup. Then prove it with a restore test, because nothing else shows a backup can be opened.

sim.title: Replay a year of Wendmoor's backups, 31 October 2025 to 14 October 2026
sim.lede: You're Mirembe, replaying the year before tonight. The figures are given data: the store holds the last 365 nightly backups, made at 01:00 from 15 October 2025 to 14 October 2026. Key v1 locked every backup before the script's first run at 00:30 on 1 November 2025; monthly rotation adds v2 that night, v3 on 1 December, and so on to v13 on 1 October 2026. Her photo is in the 180 backups of 10 November 2025 to 8 May 2026. Choose where the key lives (beside the backups, as found; the office safe, where the job holds only a public key and the private key is on paper; or a key service), how it is rotated (none; monthly, deleting old versions, as found; monthly, keeping them for opening), envelope encryption (off or on), and a weekly restore test every Sunday of the backup from 28 nights before. Step a month at a time, or run to tonight. Keys are labels such as v13, never real keys.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to tonight as found: 14 backups open, 351 cannot, her photo 0 of 180, and one stolen copy of the store exposes 14 of 365. Switch on the weekly restore test: the first fails on Sunday 2 November 2025, and 351 still cannot open. Set rotation to none: everything opens, and a stolen copy exposes 365 of 365. Choose the office safe instead: 0 exposed, but one key opens all 365 and nothing records its use. Now choose a key service, rotation keeping old versions and envelope encryption: 0 lost, 0 exposed, one leaked data key opens 1 backup.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke into the boxes. The backups were encrypted with a key kept in the same store, and a monthly rotation script deleted each old key version when it made a new one, so every backup locked with an old version became unreadable for good: 351 of 365, her photo among them. The fix is a key service that keeps keys apart from the data, rotates by adding versions and keeps the old ones for opening, with envelope encryption and regular restore tests.

steps.title: At rest and in transit: two places data needs protecting.
steps.text: Encryption in transit, TLS, protects data while it travels between computers; The Padlock covered it. Encryption at rest protects data while it sits on a disk or in a backup, so a stolen disk or a copied store shows only scrambled bytes. Both depend on the same thing: who holds the key, and where. Encryption at rest with the key stored beside the data protects against almost nothing, because whoever copies the data copies the key with it.

steps.title: Symmetric and asymmetric keys, and when each fits.
steps.text: A symmetric key locks and unlocks, like a front-door key. It is fast, so it does the heavy work of scrambling large files such as backups. An asymmetric pair splits the jobs, like a post box: the public key locks, or checks a signature, and only the private key unlocks, or signs. It is slower, so it is used for small things: proving identity in TLS, logging in with a key pair as in The Black Screen, or locking a small key for someone else. Most real systems use both: a symmetric key for the data, and something else to protect that key.

steps.title: How the rotation script lost the year, step by step.
steps.text: First, at 00:30 on the 1st, the script made a new key version and wrote it into the keys folder. Second, every backup from then on was locked with the new version. Third, the script deleted the version before, to tidy up. Fourth, at the next restore, each backup still named the version that locked it, but that version no longer existed. Step three is the mistake: rotation should stop a version locking new data, not stop it opening old data. NIST SP 800-57 makes exactly this split, with a period for applying protection and a separate one during which protected information may still be decrypted. After 12 runs only v13 was left, and only the 14 backups made under it could open.

steps.title: Envelope encryption and a key service, step by step.
steps.text: First, the backup job asks the key service for a fresh data key. Second, the service returns it twice: once plain, once locked with the master key. Third, the job scrambles the backup with the plain data key, throws the plain copy away, and stores the locked copy beside the backup. To restore, the job sends the locked data key to the service, which checks the job may ask, records the request, unlocks it with whichever master key version locked it, and hands it back. The master key never leaves the service, so a stolen store holds only locked keys, and one leaked data key opens one backup. Rotating the master key adds a version; AWS KMS keeps all earlier key material so old data keys still unlock.

steps.title: Restore tests: the only proof a backup opens.
steps.text: A checksum shows a backup hasn't changed. Only a restore shows it can be read. A restore test does the whole trip on a schedule: pick a backup, fetch its key, unlock it, read a real record, and raise an alarm if any step fails. Here a weekly test of a backup 28 nights old would have failed on Sunday 2 November 2025, the day after the first deletion, and 46 of the year's 52 would have failed. Test old backups too, not only last night's, since the oldest ones depend on the oldest key versions.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next backup. The backup job asks the key service for a data key. The key service holds master key versions v1 to v13, never lets them out, and writes each use to its record. The job stores each backup with its locked data key in the backup store. The key service locks the data keys, one per backup. The weekly restore test asks the key service to open an old data key, which it does with the version that locked it.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next backup. Each backup gets its own data key, locked by the key service's master key and kept beside it in the store. The master key never leaves the service, every unlock is recorded, and old versions stay for opening. Replayed from 31 October 2025, all 365 backups open, a stolen copy of the store exposes 0, and the weekly restore test never fails.

fix.title: The fix: keys in a key service, old versions kept, envelope encryption and restore tests
fix.text: Move the backup key into the city's key service and take it out of the backup store. Use envelope encryption: a fresh data key for every backup, locked by the master key and stored beside its backup. Keep rotating the master key every month, but by adding versions in the service, never by deleting the ones old backups need; delete a version only when no backup it locked is still kept. Allow only the backup job and the restore tool to ask the service, and read its record of each use. Add a weekly restore test that opens a real record from a backup weeks or months old, and emails someone when it fails. In the sim this gives 0 of 365 lost and 0 exposed by a stolen copy of the store. The 351 backups already lost cannot be brought back; say so to the people affected.

limits: A key service moves the risk, it doesn't remove it. Anyone allowed to ask it can unlock every backup, so who may ask, and the record of who did, matter as much as the encryption.

Keeping every version means a version that once leaked still opens what it locked. Rotation limits how much new data a leaked key can open; it doesn't re-lock old data, and AWS notes rotation does not re-encrypt data or rotate data keys.
Nothing brings back a deleted key. The 351 backups stay shut whatever the office changes now, and a key service that deletes a whole key, or imported material, can lose data the same way.

explain.seniorTake: Encryption at rest is only as good as where the key lives and how long it lives. Keep keys apart from the data they lock, ideally in a key service whose master keys never leave it and which records every use. Rotate, but understand what rotation means: a new version for new data, while the old versions stay for as long as anything they locked is kept. Deleting a key is deleting every piece of data it locked, so treat it as a data-deletion decision, with a list of what will become unreadable. Use envelope encryption so each backup has its own data key and the master key does little work and never travels. Then test restores of old backups on a schedule, because a matching checksum proves only that a file hasn't changed, not that anyone can open it.

realWorld.title: AWS KMS: rotation changes only the key for new data
realWorld.text: "Key rotation changes only the current key material, which is the cryptographic secret that is used in encryption operations. When you use the rotated KMS key to decrypt ciphertext, AWS KMS uses the key material that was used to encrypt it."

realWorld.title: AWS KMS: earlier key material is kept
realWorld.text: "AWS KMS retains all key material for a KMS key with AWS_KMS origin, even if key rotation is disabled. AWS KMS deletes key material only when you delete the KMS key." The default rotation period: "the default value is 365 days."

realWorld.title: AWS KMS: what rotation does not do
realWorld.text: "Key rotation has no effect on the data that the KMS key protects. It does not rotate the data keys that the KMS key generated or re-encrypt any data protected by the KMS key."

realWorld.title: AWS KMS: envelope encryption
realWorld.text: "Envelope encryption is the practice of encrypting plaintext data with a data key, and then encrypting the data key under another key." And: "You can safely store the encrypted data key alongside the encrypted data."

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1: key management
realWorld.text: NIST's Recommendation for Key Management, Part 1, revision 5, May 2020: "This Recommendation provides cryptographic key-management guidance."

realWorld.title: NIST: a key's cryptoperiod
realWorld.text: NIST's glossary, citing SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5: "The time span during which a specific key is authorized for use or in which the keys for a given system or application may remain in effect."

realWorld.title: NIST: the period for locking new data
realWorld.text: Originator-usage period: "The period of time in the cryptoperiod of a key during which cryptographic protection may be applied to data using that key."

realWorld.title: NIST: the period for opening old data
realWorld.text: Recipient-usage period: "The period of time during which the protected information may be processed (e.g., decrypted)." A key that has stopped locking can still be needed to open.

asked: How do you rotate keys without losing old data?
Symmetric or asymmetric: when do you use each?
interview.answer: Symmetric encryption uses one key to lock and unlock; it is fast, so it scrambles bulk data such as files, disks and backups. Asymmetric encryption uses a pair: the public key locks or verifies, the private key unlocks or signs; it is slower, so it is used for identity, as in TLS certificates and SSH logins, and for locking small things such as other keys. Envelope encryption combines them with a key service: each object gets its own symmetric data key, the data key is locked under a master key held in a key management service, and the locked data key is stored beside the data. To read, you send the locked data key to the service, which checks you are allowed, records the request, and returns the plain data key. The master key never leaves the service, a stolen store holds only locked keys, and one leaked data key exposes one object. Rotation without data loss means adding a new version for new encryptions and keeping the old versions for decryption for as long as any data they locked is kept; NIST calls these the originator-usage and recipient-usage periods, and AWS KMS keeps all earlier key material until the key is deleted. Then prove it with restore tests of old backups. A story I'd tell: a lost-property office rotated its backup key monthly with a script that deleted the old version each time, and kept the key in the same store as the backups; a year later 351 of 365 backups were unreadable, every checksum fine.

terms.def: The fictional city office in this story that keeps found items, each with a record and a photo.
The office's entry for one found item: what it is, where it was found, a photo, and the owner's name when known.
Scrambling data with a key so that only someone holding the right key can read it. Without the key it looks like nonsense.
Keeping data scrambled while it sits on a disk, in storage or in a backup, so a stolen disk or a copied store shows nothing readable.
Scrambling data while it travels between computers, such as with TLS, the padlock in the browser.
The secret value that locks and unlocks encrypted data. In this story keys are labels such as v13, never real keys.
One key that both locks and unlocks, like a front-door key. Fast, so it is used for large data such as backups.
Two matching keys, like a post box: the public key locks, and only the private key unlocks. Slower, so used for identity and small things such as other keys.
A spare copy of data kept somewhere else, to restore from after a mistake. It only counts once you have restored from it.
Copying a backup back so its data can be used again, which means unlocking it first if it is encrypted.
Where Wendmoor's nightly backups are kept: the last 365 nights. Until the fix, its keys folder held the backup key too.
A short fingerprint worked out from a file. If anything in the file changes, it no longer matches. It proves a file is unchanged, not that anyone can open it.
Swapping in a fresh key on a schedule, so a leaked key stops working for new data. Done well, the old versions are kept for opening old data.
One generation of a rotated key, such as v2 or v13. Each piece of data stays locked with the version current when it was made.
Radoslav's small program that ran at 00:30 on the 1st of each month from 1 November 2025, made a new key version, and deleted the one before.
A separate, guarded service that holds master keys, never lets them out, unlocks only for programs allowed to ask, and records each use. Also called a key management service, KMS.
Short for key management service. AWS KMS is Amazon's: its keys never leave it unencrypted, and to use one you must call the service.
Amazon Web Services: Amazon's cloud, where companies rent computers, storage and services such as AWS KMS.
A named storage container in a cloud service, such as Amazon S3, that holds files like backups.
An AWS KMS key copied into another AWS Region. A replica gets the current key material and all earlier versions, so data can be opened in either place.
The key a key service keeps for a department, used only to lock and unlock data keys. Also called a root key or key-encryption key.
A fresh key made for one backup or file. It does the scrambling, and is stored beside the data, locked by the master key.
Locking data with its own data key, then locking that data key with a master key, like a key in a sealed envelope only the key service can open.
Taking a backup all the way back to readable data on a schedule, and raising an alarm if any step fails. The only proof a backup opens.
AWS's name for the secret inside a KMS key. Rotation adds new key material; KMS keeps the earlier material to decrypt older data.
Encrypted data, the scrambled form. Plaintext is the readable form before encryption.
NIST's word for the time a key may be used. It splits into a period for locking new data and a period in which old data may still be decrypted.
In NIST SP 800-57, the part of a key's life during which it may be used to protect new data.
In NIST SP 800-57, the time during which data protected by a key may still be processed, such as decrypted. It can last long after the key stops locking.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology's Recommendation for Key Management. Part 1, revision 5 (May 2020), gives general guidance.
Information about a person who can be identified, such as an owner's name on a found-item record.
An international standard for running information security. Annex A control A.8.24 covers the use of cryptography, and A.8.13 information backup.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC6.1 covers logical access; A1.2 covers backup and recovery for availability.
The EU's General Data Protection Regulation. Article 32 asks for security suited to the risk, including encryption and the ability to restore access to data in good time.
Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act. Its protection obligation asks organisations to make reasonable security arrangements for personal data.

atWork: Pick one encrypted backup from a year ago and try to restore it, all the way to a readable record, using only your written restore steps. It is a common pattern to find encrypted backups that nobody has ever tried to restore, with keys that were rotated, replaced or deleted along the way. Then check four things. Where does each backup's key live: in a key service such as AWS KMS, or in the same bucket, disk or account as the backups? Does your rotation add versions and keep the old ones while any data they locked is kept, or does some script delete them? Do you use envelope encryption, so each backup has its own data key? And is there a scheduled restore test of old backups, not only last night's, that alerts a named person when it fails? Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.24 (use of cryptography) expects managed keys and A.8.13 (information backup) expects backups to be tested; if SOC 2, criterion CC6.1 covers logical access to keys, and A1.2 covers backup and recovery if availability is in scope. If backups hold EU residents' personal data, such as owners' names, GDPR Article 32 asks for encryption and the ability to restore access in good time; if Singapore residents', the PDPA's protection obligation does. Build it in now, with a dated record of where keys live, how versions are kept and when the last restore test passed, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: A photo-sharing startup encrypts its nightly database backups with one key file kept in the same cloud bucket as the backups. A teammate proposes a monthly job that makes a new key and deletes the old one, "so no old key can leak". What do you tell them, and what do you design instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Deleting old versions makes every backup locked with them unreadable; keep old versions for decryption as long as the backups are kept
Keep keys apart from the data, in a key management service that records each use
Use envelope encryption: a data key per backup, locked by a master key

recall.model: Rotating is good; deleting is the trap. Every backup stays locked with the version that was current when it was made, so deleting old versions makes those backups unreadable: within a year almost nothing restores. Keep old versions for decryption as long as any backup they locked is kept, and use new versions only for new backups. Also get the key out of the bucket: whoever copies the bucket now gets the backups and the key together. Put the master key in a key management service such as AWS KMS, which never lets it out, keeps earlier versions when it rotates, and records each use. Use envelope encryption: each backup gets its own data key, locked by the master key and stored beside the backup, so a stolen bucket holds only locked keys. Then schedule restores of old backups to prove they open.

options: Encrypting a backup twice with the same key
Sending encrypted data only over TLS
Locking data with its own data key, then locking that data key with a master key held elsewhere
Keeping a printed copy of the key in a sealed letter in the safe
recall.why: AWS: "Envelope encryption is the practice of encrypting plaintext data with a data key, and then encrypting the data key under another key." The locked data key can sit beside the data; the master key stays in the key service.

recall.prompt: A nightly job must lock each backup, but should never be able to open one. Which fits?
options: An asymmetric pair: the job holds only the public key, and the private key is kept elsewhere
A symmetric key stored beside the backups
A symmetric key the job reads from its own settings file
A checksum written beside each backup
recall.why: With an asymmetric pair the public key can lock but not unlock, so the job can do its work without being able to read what it wrote. A symmetric key both locks and unlocks, and a checksum locks nothing.

recall.prompt: AWS KMS rotates a key's material. What happens to data encrypted before the rotation?
options: It must be re-encrypted within 365 days
KMS keeps the earlier key material and uses it to decrypt that data automatically
It can no longer be decrypted
It is decrypted with the new key material
recall.why: AWS: "When you use the rotated KMS key to decrypt ciphertext, AWS KMS uses the key material that was used to encrypt it." KMS retains all key material for an AWS-generated key until the key itself is deleted.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Since 1 November every backup goes through the city's key service, each with its own data key, and no old version is ever deleted. The weekly restore test has passed every Sunday. In March, after a flood warning, Mr Valcourt asked for a second copy of every backup at the city's river depot across town. Radoslav now copies each night's backup and its locked data key there. Last Sunday he tried the first restore from the depot's copy, on a depot computer. It failed: the depot's computers are not allowed to ask the city's key service, which runs only in the main building.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the restore from the depot fail, and how should the second copy be set up?

keyIdeas.idea: A copy whose locked data keys can only be opened by a master key you cannot reach is useless: the key must be usable wherever you restore
Make the master key usable at the second site without putting it beside the data: a replica of the key, with all its versions, in a key service the depot may use, or a recorded permission
Test restores from the second copy on a schedule too, not only from the main store

coldCase.model: The depot's copy holds the backups and their locked data keys, but a locked data key is useless without the master key that locked it, and the depot can't reach the key service. A backup you can't unlock where you need it is only half a backup. Make the master key usable at the depot without putting it beside the data: either grant the depot's restore computer a recorded permission to ask the main key service, or, if the depot must work when the main building is down, keep a replica of the master key, with every version, in a key service the depot can use. AWS KMS multi-Region keys work this way: a replica gets the current key material and all previous versions. Then test restores from both copies on a schedule, so the next gap shows on a Sunday, not on the night you need it.
